items.text: Whether machines could ever truly be conscious is left open from the start, but the moral status of AI systems and the shape of our own self-understanding are already staked on the answer.

Before any of this uncertainty can be resolved, the pull toward seeing machines as conscious is traced to inherited biases rather than to evidence, leaving the deeper question of computation itself still unaddressed.

Having named the biases behind the intuition, the case now tests the assumption those biases lean on—computational functionalism—and finds brains, alternative dynamics, living metabolism, and simulated models all working against it.

With functionalism left shaky but not disproven, certainty about actual machine consciousness stays out of reach, so what follows is a practical reckoning with both the danger of creating it and the danger of merely seeming to face it.

Neither ruling conscious AI in nor out, what remains settled is a caution against mechanizing ourselves in AI's mirror, and an unsettled appeal to recover, in place of the algorithm, the embodied aliveness the whole inquiry has been circling.
